title: Why is DB operations in a controller bad practice? What are DAO layer benefits? How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work (@EnableAutoConfiguration, @Conditional)? How do you customize, exclude, or debug auto-configuration?
shortTitle: Why should you not put DB logic in a controller?
keyPoints: Controller handles HTTP parsing and response formatting, Service handles business logic, Repository handles data access
Putting database code in a controller violates separation of concerns and makes testing impossible without a running database
The DAO pattern abstracts persistence so you can swap the database without changing the service layer
Auto-configuration reads classpath and properties, then creates beans via @Conditional annotations
@ConditionalOnMissingBean ensures your custom @Bean always overrides auto-configured defaults
Debug auto-configuration with --debug flag or /actuator/conditions endpoint to see why beans were created or skipped

s1_definition.oneliner: Controller handles HTTP, Service handles business logic, Repository handles data access, and auto-configuration creates beans automatically based on classpath and properties via @Conditional annotations.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Layered architecture** – Spring Boot applications follow Controller to Service to Repository layering where each layer has a single responsibility.
- **Controller** – receives HTTP requests, validates input, delegates to the Service layer, and formats the HTTP response.
- **Service** – contains business logic such as interest calculation, validation rules, and transaction orchestration.
- **Repository (DAO)** – abstracts all data access behind an interface so the database engine can be swapped without changing business logic.
- **Auto-configuration** – Spring Boot scans the classpath and properties at startup, then uses `@Conditional` annotations to decide which beans to create automatically.
- **@ConditionalOnMissingBean** – ensures that your custom `@Bean` definition always takes priority over the auto-configured default.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, the receptionist (controller) greets customers and routes them to the right desk. The loan officer (service) calculates EMI amounts and applies business rules. The vault keeper (repository) stores and retrieves records from the safe. The receptionist never opens the vault directly. Auto-configuration is like the branch manager who walks in on the first day, sees vault equipment already in the building, and automatically sets up the vault without anyone filling out a checklist.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  HTTP Request
       │
       ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │     Controller Layer         │
  │  @RestController             │
  │  Parse request, validate,    │
  │  format response             │
  └──────────┬──────────────────┘
             │ delegates
             ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │     Service Layer            │
  │  @Service + @Transactional   │
  │  Business logic, rules,      │
  │  orchestration               │
  └──────────┬──────────────────┘
             │ delegates
             ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │     Repository Layer         │
  │  @Repository / JpaRepository │
  │  SQL, queries, data access   │
  └──────────┬──────────────────┘
             │
             ▼
        [ Database ]
```

```text
  Auto-Configuration Decision Flow:

  classpath has DataSource.class?
       │
       ├── NO  → skip DataSourceAutoConfiguration
       │
       └── YES → spring.datasource.url set?
                    │
                    ├── NO  → skip (no property)
                    │
                    └── YES → user defined @Bean DataSource?
                                 │
                                 ├── YES → back off (@ConditionalOnMissingBean)
                                 │
                                 └── NO  → create HikariCP DataSource bean
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Layered architecture separates concerns so that each part of the application has one job. The Controller handles HTTP: parsing request parameters, validating input shapes, and formatting JSON responses. The Service handles business logic: calculating interest, enforcing transfer limits, and coordinating multi-step operations inside a transaction. The Repository handles data access: running queries and mapping results to objects. When Rajesh puts a JPA query inside a Controller at National Bank of India, the code becomes untestable without a database, unreusable by other classes, and impossible to manage transactions correctly.

Spring Boot auto-configuration is the engine that creates beans based on what it finds on the classpath and in your properties. When you add `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` to your dependencies and set `spring.datasource.url`, auto-configuration creates a HikariCP connection pool, an EntityManagerFactory, and a TransactionManager, all without a single explicit `@Bean` definition. The `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` annotation ensures that if you define your own DataSource, the auto-configured one steps aside. Debug with `--debug` to see exactly why each auto-configuration class matched or was skipped.

Remember one sentence: the Controller parses HTTP, the Service applies business rules, the Repository talks to the database, and auto-configuration wires it all together based on your classpath and properties.
